es: Analizar la tesis, la postura, los recursos retóricos y las implicaciones de un artículo de opinión largo.

teaching.en: The thesis is the main claim of an article: children should be bored sometimes.
teaching.es: La tesis es la afirmación central de un artículo: los niños deberían aburrirse a veces.
teaching.explanationEs: Suele aparecer al principio y es lo que el autor defiende, no lo que admite.
segments: The thesis is the main claim of
an article: children should be bored sometimes.
teaching.audioText: The thesis is the main claim of an article: children should be bored sometimes.

teaching.en: The stance is clear from the verbs: I would argue, I am convinced, it seems to me.
teaching.es: La postura se ve en los verbos: yo diría, estoy convencido, me parece.
teaching.explanationEs: Los verbos de postura y los matices (would, seems) indican cuánta seguridad tiene el autor.
segments: The stance is clear from the verbs: I would
argue, I am convinced, it seems to me.
teaching.audioText: The stance is clear from the verbs: I would argue, I am convinced, it seems to me.

teaching.en: Writers concede a point before they answer it: Much as I understand the worry, the evidence points the other way.
teaching.es: Quien escribe concede un punto antes de responderlo: Aunque entiendo la preocupación, la evidencia apunta en sentido contrario.
teaching.explanationEs: Conceder no cambia la postura: prepara el terreno para la refutación.
segments: Writers concede a point before they answer it: Much as
I understand the worry, the evidence points the other way.
teaching.audioText: Writers concede a point before they answer it: Much as I understand the worry, the evidence points the other way.

teaching.en: A rhetorical question does not ask for information: What, then, should adults do?
teaching.es: Una pregunta retórica no pide información: ¿Qué deberían hacer, entonces, los adultos?
teaching.explanationEs: Empuja al lector a seguir el razonamiento del autor y a llegar a su misma respuesta.
segments: A rhetorical question does not ask for
information: What, then, should adults do?
teaching.audioText: A rhetorical question does not ask for information: What, then, should adults do?

teaching.en: The implication of a sentence is what it suggests without saying it.
teaching.es: La implicación de una frase es lo que sugiere sin decirlo.
teaching.explanationEs: Para detectarla pregúntate: si esto es cierto, ¿qué quiere que piense el lector?
segments: The implication of a sentence is
what it suggests without saying it.
teaching.audioText: The implication of a sentence is what it suggests without saying it.

teaching.en: Children whose minds wander often invent games, and boredom may be the start.
teaching.es: Los niños cuya mente divaga suelen inventar juegos, y el aburrimiento puede ser el comienzo.
teaching.explanationEs: Often y may son cautelas: el autor no afirma que ocurra siempre.
segments: Children whose minds wander often invent games,
and boredom may be the start.
teaching.audioText: Children whose minds wander often invent games, and boredom may be the start.

prompt.es: ¿Cuál es la tesis de este párrafo?

choices.text: Children who are never bored miss something important.
Nobody enjoys a long afternoon with nothing to do.
Children should have more time with screens.

feedback.es: La tesis es lo que el autor defiende tras «yet I would argue»; lo anterior es solo lo que admite.

hint.es: La tesis es la afirmación que defiende, no la que admite al principio.

origin.text: Nobody enjoys a long afternoon with nothing to do, yet I would argue that children who are never bored miss something important.

prompt.es: Completa: «Quien escribe concede un punto antes de rebatirlo.»

answer.text: concede

feedback.es: Conceder es admitir una parte de la razón al otro antes de responderle.

hint.es: Verbo que admite la razón del otro sin cambiar de postura.

origin.text: Writers ___ a point before they answer it.

prompt.es: Ordena: «Los niños aburridos suelen inventar juegos y hacer mejores preguntas.»

answer.text: Bored children tend to invent games and ask better questions

feedback.es: Tend to + verbo base es una cautela: el autor no dice que siempre ocurra.

hint.es: El sujeto va primero; tend to lleva el verbo en forma base.

prompt.es: ¿Cuál es la postura del autor ante la objeción de los padres?

choices.text: He fully agrees with the parents.
He concedes the worry but disagrees with it.
He ignores the parents' objection.

feedback.es: Much as I understand reconoce la preocupación, pero la evidencia «points the other way»: la rechaza.

origin.text: Some parents will object that boredom is a waste of time. Much as I understand the worry, the evidence points the other way.

prompt.es: Escucha y elige qué efecto busca la pregunta retórica del autor.

choices.text: It asks listeners for information.
It changes the subject completely.
It pushes listeners to follow the writer's answer.

feedback.es: El autor responde él mismo a su pregunta («Nothing, mostly»): es retórica y guía al lector hacia su tesis.

origin.audio: What, then, should adults do? Nothing, mostly. Hand over the tablet and the problem is solved in a minute. Leave the silence alone, and something more interesting may grow.

prompt.es: Relaciona cada frase del artículo con su función.

pairs: Is that really too much to ask?
For example, a box can become a ship

feedback.es: Cada frase cumple un papel distinto en el análisis: postura, concesión, pregunta retórica, cautela y ejemplo.

pairs: Is that really too much to ask?
For example, a box can become a ship

prompt.es: ¿Qué implica el autor en la última frase del artículo?

choices.text: Constant activity may leave children less able to reflect.
Children must never use screens.
Adults should stop working.

feedback.es: El autor no lo dice abiertamente, pero sugiere que quien nunca se queda a solas tendrá dificultades para concentrarse.

origin.text: It would be wrong to think that every child will turn a quiet hour into a masterpiece. Nevertheless, children who have never learned to sit with themselves may find it hard to sit with anything else.

prompt.es: Completa: «No se afirma que sea siempre agradable; se afirma que es productivo.»

answer.text: claimed

feedback.es: El autor repite claim para marcar con precisión lo que sí y lo que no defiende.

origin.text: It is not claimed that boredom is always nice; it is ___ that it is often productive.

prompt.es: Escucha y elige cuánta seguridad muestra el autor sobre los estudios.

choices.text: He is certain that the studies prove everything.
He is careful about how far the evidence goes.
He doubts that any study exists.

feedback.es: Suggest, tend to y «does not mean every child will» son cautelas: el autor limita su afirmación.

origin.audio: Several studies suggest that bored children tend to invent games, draw and ask better questions. Of course, that does not mean every bored child will.

prompt.es: Escribe una concesión que mantenga la postura del autor sobre los estudios.

answer.text: Much as I accept that the studies are few, the evidence still points to a benefit.
accepted: Much as I accept that the studies are few, the evidence still points to a benefit.
Although the studies are few, the evidence still points to a benefit.
Few though the studies are, the evidence points to a benefit.
Much as I accept that there are few studies, the evidence suggests a benefit.

feedback.es: Much as reconoce el límite de los estudios y la oración principal mantiene la postura, sin but.

origin.text: El autor admite que hay pocos estudios, pero mantiene que la evidencia apunta a un beneficio. Escríbelo en una sola frase con Much as…

prompt.es: ¿Qué efecto tiene «tend to» en esta afirmación?

choices.text: It makes the claim completely certain.
It turns the claim into a question.
It makes the claim cautious, not absolute.

feedback.es: Tend to presenta una tendencia habitual, no una ley sin excepciones: es una forma de cautela.

origin.text: Bored children tend to draw more.

prompt.es: Ordena: «La tesis es la afirmación central del artículo.»

answer.text: The thesis is the main claim of the article

feedback.es: La definición usa is para equiparar la tesis con la afirmación principal.

prompt.es: Resume en inglés la tesis del artículo con un verbo de postura.

answer.text: The author argues that children should be bored sometimes.
accepted: The author argues that children should be bored sometimes.
The writer claims that bored children become more creative.
The author maintains that bored children invent more games.
The writer believes that children need to be bored sometimes.

feedback.es: Un verbo de postura (argues, claims, maintains) atribuye la tesis al autor en lugar de presentarla como un hecho.

origin.text: Artículo «Let Them Be Bored». El autor defiende que los niños deben aburrirse a veces porque así inventan y reflexionan más.

title.es: Proyecto de escritura: edición de precisión

es: Editar un borrador con precisión: corregir tiempos, registro, cohesión, conectores y concisión eligiendo el cambio mínimo.

teaching.en: We edit in layers: first the meaning, then the cohesion, then the wording.
teaching.es: Editamos por capas: primero el significado, luego la cohesión y después la redacción.
teaching.explanationEs: Revisar todo a la vez hace perder errores; cada capa tiene su pregunta.
segments: We edit in layers: first the meaning,
then the cohesion, then the wording.
teaching.audioText: We edit in layers: first the meaning, then the cohesion, then the wording.

teaching.en: A connector must match the logic: We lowered the price; as a result, sales rose.
teaching.es: Un conector debe respetar la lógica: Bajamos el precio; como resultado, las ventas subieron.
teaching.explanationEs: Suma (moreover), contrasta (however) o da resultado (as a result): elige según la relación real.
segments: A connector must match the logic: We lowered
the price; as a result, sales rose.
teaching.audioText: A connector must match the logic: We lowered the price; as a result, sales rose.

teaching.en: A wordy sentence hides its point: In order to finish, we need time becomes To finish, we need time.
teaching.es: Una frase prolija esconde su idea: In order to finish, we need time pasa a To finish, we need time.
teaching.explanationEs: Si puedes quitar palabras sin perder significado, la frase estaba inflada.
segments: A wordy sentence hides its point: In order to finish,
we need time becomes To finish, we need time.
teaching.audioText: A wordy sentence hides its point: In order to finish, we need time becomes To finish, we need time.

teaching.en: Good writers tighten a sentence by cutting repetition: the newly opened shop, not the new, recently opened shop.
teaching.es: Quien escribe bien ajusta una frase eliminando repeticiones: the newly opened shop, no the new, recently opened shop.
teaching.explanationEs: New y recently opened dicen lo mismo: un solo adverbio basta.
segments: Good writers tighten a sentence by cutting repetition: the
newly opened shop, not the new, recently opened shop.
teaching.audioText: Good writers tighten a sentence by cutting repetition: the newly opened shop, not the new, recently opened shop.

teaching.en: Keep the tense steady: When the manager arrived, the team had already finished.
teaching.es: Mantén estable el tiempo verbal: Cuando llegó el jefe, el equipo ya había terminado.
teaching.explanationEs: Lo anterior a otro hecho pasado lleva had + participio; no mezcles tiempos sin motivo.
segments: Keep the tense steady: When the manager
arrived, the team had already finished.
teaching.audioText: Keep the tense steady: When the manager arrived, the team had already finished.

teaching.en: A vague phrase such as a lot of weakens a report; a large number of is more exact.
teaching.es: Una expresión vaga como a lot of debilita un informe; a large number of es más exacta.
teaching.explanationEs: El registro académico y profesional prefiere cantidades o expresiones precisas.
segments: A vague phrase such as a lot of weakens
a report; a large number of is more exact.
teaching.audioText: A vague phrase such as a lot of weakens a report; a large number of is more exact.

prompt.es: Marca 1: elige el conector que respeta la lógica.

choices.text: however
as a result
on the other hand

feedback.es: Terminar pronto es la consecuencia del esfuerzo; however y on the other hand marcan contraste.

hint.es: El segundo hecho es la consecuencia del primero.

origin.text: The team worked hard all week; ___, they finished the report early.

prompt.es: Completa: «A pesar de la lluvia, terminamos la encuesta.»

answer.text: the

feedback.es: Despite se une directamente al nombre, con su determinante y sin of: despite the rain.

hint.es: Despite va seguido del nombre; este necesita su determinante.

origin.text: Despite ___ rain, we finished the survey.

prompt.es: Ordena: «Además de la encuesta, realizamos entrevistas.»

answer.text: In addition to the survey, we held interviews

feedback.es: In addition to + nombre añade información y abre la frase, seguido de coma.

hint.es: Empieza por la expresión que añade información.

prompt.es: Marca 4: ¿qué versión es más concisa y precisa?

choices.text: The match was postponed because of the fact that there was rain.
Since the rain had fallen, the match was postponed.
Because it rained, the match was postponed.

feedback.es: Because dice lo mismo que due to the fact that con menos palabras y sin cambiar el sentido.

origin.text: Due to the fact that it rained, the match was postponed.

prompt.es: Escucha y elige qué hace la editora con la frase del borrador.

choices.text: She replaces a vague phrase with an exact one.
She adds a connector of contrast.
She moves the sentence to the end.

feedback.es: La editora cambia a lot of por una cifra: un registro profesional exige expresiones precisas.

origin.audio: The draft said: We did a lot of interviews. The editor changed it to: We carried out forty interviews. She explained that a lot of is vague, while forty is exact.

prompt.es: Relaciona cada conector con la relación lógica que expresa.

feedback.es: Elegir bien el conector depende de la lógica: suma, contraste, resultado o ejemplo.

prompt.es: Marca 9: corrige el conector para expresar un resultado.

answer.text: The prices were lower; consequently, sales rose.
accepted: The prices were lower; consequently, sales rose.
The prices were lower; therefore, sales rose.
The prices were lower, so sales rose.
The prices were lower; as a result, sales rose.
The prices were lower; thus, sales rose.
The prices were lower; hence, sales rose.
The prices were lower; for this reason, sales rose.

feedback.es: Las ventas suben a causa de los precios bajos: hace falta un conector de resultado, no de contraste.

origin.text: The prices were lower; however, sales rose.

prompt.es: Completa: «Le agradeceríamos que enviara el informe para el lunes.»

answer.text: could

feedback.es: En un registro formal, la petición se suaviza con if you could + verbo base.

origin.text: We would be grateful if you ___ send the report by Monday.

prompt.es: Escucha y elige qué corrige la editora en el borrador.

choices.text: She replaces the verb with a more formal word.
She adds a form that shows which event came first.
She removes a repeated word.

feedback.es: Había terminado ocurrió antes de la llegada: had finished ordena los dos hechos pasados.

origin.audio: The draft said: When the director arrived, we already finished the report. The editor says the verb should be had finished, because the report was completed before the director came.

prompt.es: Marca 12: ¿a qué se refiere «Such a habit»?

choices.text: To clear rules.
To distraction only.
To using phones in class.

feedback.es: Such a habit retoma la costumbre descrita en la primera frase: usar el móvil en clase.

origin.text: Many students use phones in class. This leads to distraction. Such a habit can be reduced with clear rules.

prompt.es: Marca 6: quita la repetición sin perder información.

choices.text: The newly opened shop is very popular.
The shop is very popular.
The new and recently opened shop is very popular.

feedback.es: Newly opened resume new y recently opened; quitar ambos borraría información y mantenerlos repite la idea.

origin.text: The new, recently opened shop is very popular.

prompt.es: Ordena: «Editamos primero el significado y después la redacción.»

answer.text: We edit the meaning first and then the wording
accepted: We edit the meaning first and then the wording
First we edit the meaning and then the wording
We first edit the meaning and then the wording

feedback.es: Las capas de la revisión se ordenan con first y then: primero el sentido, después la forma.

prompt.es: Marca 11: sustituye la frase coloquial por una de registro neutro.

answer.text: The manager was annoyed because the report was late.
accepted: The manager was annoyed because the report was late.
The director was upset because the report was late.
The manager was displeased because the report was late.
The boss was annoyed because the report was delayed.

feedback.es: En un informe se evita got really mad: un adjetivo neutro (annoyed, upset) mantiene el sentido con más formalidad.

origin.text: The boss got really mad because the report was late.

evidenceGroups: because the report was submitted late

es: Valorar una actuación oral modelo con una rúbrica de cuatro criterios: estructura, precisión, tacto y evidencia.

teaching.en: A rubric lists the criteria we use to assess a performance.
teaching.es: Una rúbrica enumera los criterios que usamos para valorar una actuación.
teaching.explanationEs: Valorar con criterios evita las impresiones vagas del tipo «me gustó».
segments: A rubric lists the criteria we
use to assess a performance.
teaching.audioText: A rubric lists the criteria we use to assess a performance.

teaching.en: The first criterion is structure: a clear opening, two reasons and a closing.
teaching.es: El primer criterio es la estructura: una apertura clara, dos razones y un cierre.
teaching.explanationEs: Se comprueba con las señales de orden: first, second, finally, to sum up.
segments: The first criterion is structure: a clear
opening, two reasons and a closing.
teaching.audioText: The first criterion is structure: a clear opening, two reasons and a closing.

teaching.en: The second criterion is accuracy: the verbs, connectors and word order must be correct.
teaching.es: El segundo criterio es la precisión: los verbos, los conectores y el orden de las palabras deben ser correctos.
teaching.explanationEs: Es la capa que repasaste en la clase de edición de precisión.
segments: The second criterion is accuracy: the verbs,
connectors and word order must be correct.
teaching.audioText: The second criterion is accuracy: the verbs, connectors and word order must be correct.

teaching.en: The third is tact: a good speaker concedes a point and softens a request.
teaching.es: El tercero es el tacto: quien habla bien concede un punto y suaviza una petición.
teaching.explanationEs: Much as…, I was wondering whether… y should it fail son señales de tacto.
segments: The third is tact: a good speaker
concedes a point and softens a request.
teaching.audioText: The third is tact: a good speaker concedes a point and softens a request.

teaching.en: The fourth criterion is evidence: a strong speaker supports each reason with data.
teaching.es: El cuarto criterio es la evidencia: quien habla con fuerza apoya cada razón con datos.
teaching.explanationEs: Una encuesta, una cifra o un ejemplo concreto valen más que «mucha gente lo piensa».
segments: The fourth criterion is evidence: a strong
speaker supports each reason with data.
teaching.audioText: The fourth criterion is evidence: a strong speaker supports each reason with data.

teaching.en: A strength is something the speaker does well; a weakness is something to improve.
teaching.es: Una fortaleza es algo que la persona hace bien; una debilidad es algo que debe mejorar.
teaching.explanationEs: Una buena valoración nombra ambas y cita la frase que lo demuestra.
segments: A strength is something the speaker does
well; a weakness is something to improve.
teaching.audioText: A strength is something the speaker does well; a weakness is something to improve.

prompt.es: ¿Qué criterio de la rúbrica se aprecia en esta apertura y cierre?

choices.text: Accuracy
Evidence
Structure

feedback.es: Una apertura clara y un cierre que resume ordenan el discurso: es el criterio de estructura.

hint.es: Apertura y cierre ordenan el discurso; no corrigen verbos.

origin.text: Opening: I would like to argue that the library should open until nine. Closing: So, to sum up, longer hours will help students.

prompt.es: Completa: «Una fortaleza es algo que la persona hace bien.»

answer.text: strength

feedback.es: Strength es lo que la persona hace bien; lo que debe mejorar se llama weakness.

origin.text: A ___ is something the speaker does well.

prompt.es: Ordena: «El segundo criterio es la precisión.»

answer.text: The second criterion is accuracy

feedback.es: La enumeración de criterios usa ordinales y el verbo is: The second criterion is accuracy.

hint.es: Empieza por The second; al final va el nombre del criterio.

prompt.es: Escucha y elige qué criterio demuestra esta parte de la intervención.

choices.text: Tact: she concedes a point and softens a request.
Structure: she gives a closing summary.
Accuracy: she corrects a verb error.

feedback.es: Much as I appreciate concede el punto y I was wondering whether suaviza la petición: es tacto.

origin.audio: Much as I appreciate the staff's concern about costs, I believe volunteers could help. I was wondering whether we could try it for three months.

prompt.es: ¿Qué criterio demuestra esta frase de la actuación modelo?

choices.text: Tact
Evidence
Structure

feedback.es: Una encuesta con una cifra concreta apoya la razón con datos: es evidencia.

origin.text: A survey of two hundred students shows that most of them study in the evening.

prompt.es: Relaciona cada criterio con la señal que lo demuestra.

feedback.es: Cada criterio tiene su propia señal observable: valorar es buscarla en las frases del texto.

prompt.es: Escucha y elige una fortaleza real de la actuación.

choices.text: She avoids any contingency plan.
She speaks without an opening.
She supports her reasons with data.

feedback.es: La oradora cita una encuesta con una cifra: esa evidencia sostiene su primera razón.

origin.audio: I would like to argue that the town needs a night bus. First, a survey of three hundred residents shows that many workers finish after midnight. Second, much as I appreciate the council's worry about costs, a pilot route would be cheap. Finally, I was wondering whether we could begin in spring. Should it fail, we will stop after three months.

prompt.es: ¿Qué criterio falla más en esta intervención?

choices.text: Tact
Structure
Accuracy

feedback.es: La estructura es clara (first, second, finally), pero ordenar pagar y rechazar objeciones carece de tacto.

origin.text: First, I would like to propose a night bus. Second, you must pay for it, and I will not listen to objections. Finally, there is no other option.

prompt.es: Completa: «Usó conectores y verbos incorrectos, así que su precisión fue baja.»

answer.text: accuracy

feedback.es: Los conectores y los verbos incorrectos bajan el criterio de precisión, no el de estructura ni el de tacto.

origin.text: She used the wrong connectors and verb forms, so her ___ was low.

prompt.es: Valora la intervención: escribe una fortaleza y una debilidad con evidencia.

answer.text: One strength is the evidence: she mentions a survey. One weakness is tact, because she never concedes a point.
accepted: One strength is the evidence: she mentions a survey. One weakness is tact, because she never concedes a point.
Her main strength is the evidence: she quotes a survey. Her weakness is tact, because she never concedes a point.
One strength is the structure: she says first and second. One weakness is that she gives no evidence for the second reason.

feedback.es: Una valoración completa nombra una fortaleza y una debilidad y cita en qué frase se ve cada una.

origin.text: First, a survey shows that most residents use the bus. Second, a pilot route would be cheap. So, we should try it.

prompt.es: ¿Qué comentario valora con evidencia y no solo con impresión?

choices.text: I liked it a lot.
Her structure is clear: she says first, second and finally.
She seemed a nice person.

feedback.es: Un buen comentario nombra el criterio y cita las señales concretas (first, second, finally).

prompt.es: Ordena: «Concede un punto y suaviza su petición.»

answer.text: She concedes a point and softens her request

feedback.es: Los dos verbos en tercera persona describen las dos señales de tacto que se observan.

prompt.es: Completa: «Para valorar con justicia, citamos las palabras exactas.»

answer.text: assess

feedback.es: Assess fairly significa valorar con criterios y apoyarse en las palabras exactas como evidencia.

origin.text: To ___ fairly, we quote the exact words.

es: Redactar en tiempo limitado una respuesta completa con postura, ejemplo, concesión, refutación breve y autocorrección documentada.

vocabulary.es: más bien (or rather: o mejor dicho)

teaching.en: In a timed answer, a short outline saves minutes: stance, example, concession, closing.
teaching.es: En una respuesta cronometrada, un esquema breve ahorra minutos: postura, ejemplo, concesión y cierre.
teaching.explanationEs: Dos minutos de esquema evitan rehacer el texto a mitad de camino.
segments: In a timed answer, a short outline
saves minutes: stance, example, concession, closing.
teaching.audioText: In a timed answer, a short outline saves minutes: stance, example, concession, closing.

teaching.en: A clear stance needs nuance: I would argue that remote work helps, at least for focused tasks.
teaching.es: Una postura clara necesita matiz: yo diría que el trabajo remoto ayuda, al menos en tareas de concentración.
teaching.explanationEs: I would argue y at least suavizan la afirmación sin debilitar la postura.
segments: A clear stance needs nuance: I would argue that
remote work helps, at least for focused tasks.
teaching.audioText: A clear stance needs nuance: I would argue that remote work helps, at least for focused tasks.

teaching.en: A concession can be short: Admittedly, open offices are friendly.
teaching.es: Una concesión puede ser breve: Es cierto que las oficinas abiertas son agradables.
teaching.explanationEs: Admittedly reconoce un punto ajeno; después puedes refutarlo con but o however.
segments: A concession can be short:
Admittedly, open offices are friendly.
teaching.audioText: A concession can be short: Admittedly, open offices are friendly.

teaching.en: When a sentence is unclear, rephrase it: It helps, or rather, it helps some people.
teaching.es: Cuando una frase no queda clara, reformúlala: Ayuda, o mejor dicho, ayuda a algunas personas.
teaching.explanationEs: Or rather corrige a la vista del lector y deja documentada tu autocorrección.
segments: When a sentence is unclear, rephrase it: It
helps, or rather, it helps some people.
teaching.audioText: When a sentence is unclear, rephrase it: It helps, or rather, it helps some people.

teaching.en: What I mean is that focus matters; let me clarify this before I continue.
teaching.es: Lo que quiero decir es que la concentración importa; permíteme aclararlo antes de seguir.
teaching.explanationEs: What I mean is y let me clarify son otras fórmulas para precisar lo que acabas de decir.
segments: What I mean is that focus matters;
let me clarify this before I continue.
teaching.audioText: What I mean is that focus matters; let me clarify this before I continue.

teaching.en: After the last sentence, I revise once: I check the tense, the connectors and the tone.
teaching.es: Después de la última frase, reviso una vez: compruebo el tiempo verbal, los conectores y el tono.
teaching.explanationEs: Reserva el último minuto para esta revisión final: es donde se ganan puntos de precisión.

prompt.es: Responde al caso con postura, ejemplo, concesión y autocorrección (unas 150 palabras).

answer.text: I would argue that schools should limit phones in class, but not ban them completely. For example, in my cousin's school the students keep their phones in a box during lessons, and the teachers say that the pupils now listen more carefully. Admittedly, phones can be useful: a dictionary, a map or a camera can help with a project. Much as I respect that view, the evidence I have seen points to another conclusion, because when a phone is on the desk, it is hard to ignore. The benefits depend on rules, or rather, on clear rules that everyone understands. What I mean is that the problem is not the phone itself but the moment when it is used. Schools could allow phones for specific tasks and keep them away during explanations and exams. Some parents worry about emergencies, so the school office should always be available by telephone. On balance, a limited and well-explained rule would help pupils to concentrate without feeling punished.
accepted: I would argue that schools should limit phones in class, but not ban them completely. For example, in my cousin's school the students keep their phones in a box during lessons, and the teachers say that the pupils now listen more carefully. Admittedly, phones can be useful: a dictionary, a map or a camera can help with a project. Much as I respect that view, the evidence I have seen points to another conclusion, because when a phone is on the desk, it is hard to ignore. The benefits depend on rules, or rather, on clear rules that everyone understands. What I mean is that the problem is not the phone itself but the moment when it is used. Schools could allow phones for specific tasks and keep them away during explanations and exams. Some parents worry about emergencies, so the school office should always be available by telephone. On balance, a limited and well-explained rule would help pupils to concentrate without feeling punished.

In my opinion, phones should stay in the bag during lessons. Take my own class: last year, we used to check messages all the time, and the teacher had to repeat every explanation twice. It is true that phones can help with research, and I do not want a total ban. Even though a quick search can save time, it also opens a hundred distractions. To put it more precisely, a phone is useful only when the teacher asks for it. Let me rephrase that: a phone is a tool, not a toy, and a tool needs a purpose. For instance, the class could use phones for a short quiz and then put them away. That is a fair compromise. Some students may feel nervous without their phones, but they would soon notice how much they can concentrate. All in all, a clear and limited rule is better than a total ban or complete freedom. Students need trust, and they also need help.

answer.text: Years ago, I used to believe that I would never speak English well. I had never spoken with a stranger in English, and I was afraid of making mistakes. Then I started studying with an app every morning, and my confidence slowly grew. The article says that students who learn with apps never speak well. Admittedly, an app alone may not be enough: it cannot give you a real conversation. Much as I respect the author, I would argue that the claim is too strong. The source seems to rely on a small survey, and it gives no data about students who also talk with people, so its conclusion may not be reliable. I was wondering whether the author could explain how many students took part. I understand that a short article has little space, and I appreciate the concern about speaking well. Revision: I wrote that apps are useless for speaking, or rather, I should say that they are useful but not enough. On balance, the best plan is an app plus real conversations, and that is exactly what this course has given me.
accepted: Years ago, I used to believe that I would never speak English well. I had never spoken with a stranger in English, and I was afraid of making mistakes. Then I started studying with an app every morning, and my confidence slowly grew. The article says that students who learn with apps never speak well. Admittedly, an app alone may not be enough: it cannot give you a real conversation. Much as I respect the author, I would argue that the claim is too strong. The source seems to rely on a small survey, and it gives no data about students who also talk with people, so its conclusion may not be reliable. I was wondering whether the author could explain how many students took part. I understand that a short article has little space, and I appreciate the concern about speaking well. Revision: I wrote that apps are useless for speaking, or rather, I should say that they are useful but not enough. On balance, the best plan is an app plus real conversations, and that is exactly what this course has given me.

When I was a child, I would watch films in English without understanding a word, and my cousin used to laugh at me. Later, I had to take an exam, and that was the moment when I decided to learn properly. An online post claims that apps are a waste of time. It is true that an app cannot replace a teacher. Even though I agree with part of that view, I think the post may be wrong, because it gives no numbers and does not say who wrote it. The source seems weak, so I would be careful before believing it. I was wondering whether the author has ever used an app for a full year. With respect, one experience does not prove a rule. I appreciate that some people learn better with a teacher, and I see your point. Let me rephrase my conclusion: apps do not teach everything, but they help you to start. In the end, I changed my opinion only a little, and this course helped me to explain why.
